To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The gut fungal microbiota is dysbiotic in Crohn’s disease patients.

the fungal microbiome in the inflamed intestinal mucosa was distinguishable from the noninflammed area in patients with active Crohn’s disease, and that the fungal diversity in both inflamed and noninflammed mucosal samples was associated with the expression level of pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines in CD patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of gut fungal microbiome in the pathogenesis and development of CD.
the fungal microbiota of the inflamed mucosal tissue in CD patients.
the study of the fungal microbiomes in patients with CD and the relationship between the fungal microbiota and the disease activity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
dysbiosis of the mucosal and fecal fungal community in CD patients is associated with mucosal and systemic inflammation.
dysbiosis of gut fungal microbiome is associated with inflammation in CD.
the fungal community is altered in CD, and dysbiosis of fungal microbiota may contribute to the pathogenesis of the disease.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the fungal microbiome of the inflamed intestinal mucosa is different from that of the normal mucosa in CD patients.
gut fungal microbiota dysbiosis was associated with mucosal inflammatory response in CD.
the gut fungal microbiota is altered in CD patients and is associated with the severity of disease activity and mucosal inflammation, which might contribute to the development of the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are differences in the fungal microbiota between inflamed and noninflamed areas of Crohn’s disease patients.
gut fungi may play a role in CD pathogenesis.
there are differences in the fungal microbiota of the inflamed mucosal area compared with the non-inflamed area in CD.
